## Simple explanation

A random forest combines the opinions of many decision trees. Each tree
learns from a slightly different view of the training data, and their
combined prediction is often more reliable than an individual tree.

## Technical explanation

A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees trained with
bootstrapped samples and randomized feature subsets. Classification usually
aggregates votes or class probabilities; regression commonly averages tree
outputs. Randomization reduces correlation among trees, which can reduce
ensemble variance.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Random forests are strong, relatively low-maintenance baselines for
structured data. They capture nonlinear relationships and feature
interactions without feature scaling, although large forests can require
substantial memory and are less straightforward to interpret than a single
tree.

## How it works

Each tree is fitted on a sample drawn with replacement. At each split, the
tree considers a random subset of features and selects a useful split.
Predictions are combined across trees; out-of-bag examples can provide an
internal performance estimate when bootstrap sampling is used.

## Practical example

For predicting whether a loan application will default, a random forest can
combine many trees trained on applicant features. Evaluate it on a
held-out, representative split and inspect class-specific metrics rather
than relying on training accuracy alone.

## Common misconceptions

- A forest is not automatically unbiased or fair; it can reproduce
  limitations in the data and target.
- Feature importance scores are not causal explanations and can be biased
  by feature properties or correlated inputs.
